requirements.requirement: Provide an encrypted volume mounted at /srv/secure on node1
requirements.summary: A LUKS2-encrypted loopback-backed volume was created (cryptsetup luksFormat over a loop device backed by /var/lib/luks/secure.img), opened as /dev/mapper/secure, formatted ext4, and mounted at /srv/secure. cryptsetup status confirmed LUKS2/aes-xts-plain64 in active read/write use, and a test file write/read succeeded.

requirements.requirement: Volume unlocks automatically at boot with no interactive input
requirements.summary: A root-only keyfile (/etc/keys/secure.key, mode 400) was configured in /etc/conf.d/dmcrypt (target/loop_file/key) and the dmcrypt OpenRC service was enabled in the boot runlevel, allowing unattended unlock. Across three real reboots the volume was found unlocked (cryptsetup status active) without any interactive prompt, confirming non-interactive automatic unlock.

requirements.requirement: Volume mounts automatically (read-write, at /srv/secure) at boot, demonstrated across a real restart cycle with pre/post healthy state and data persistence
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id a8f9af85 with /srv/secure mounted rw and dmcrypt/localmount started. A real reboot was performed (ack returned, connection dropped/reconnected, new boot_id 75d7c854), after which the mount was found read-only — a genuine bug, diagnosed via dmesg (loop file attached before root fs was remounted rw) and fixed by adding rc_after/rc_need=root. A second reboot (boot_id 275d40ab) revealed a related ordering bug (volume unlocked but not auto-mounted at /srv/secure), refined by scoping rc_after to only 'root'. A third reboot (boot_id ad3dd09e, matching the fixed global after-executor boot-identity snapshot) showed the volume auto-unlocked, auto-mounted read-write at /srv/secure, and previously written test data intact, with dmcrypt+localmount both 'started' — completing a full healthy→disruption→restoration transition with the final state working correctly.

overall_summary: The task — an encrypted volume at /srv/secure on node1 that unlocks and mounts unattended at boot — is satisfied. The executor built a LUKS2 volume with keyfile-based unattended unlock via OpenRC's dmcrypt service, then validated the requirement with three real, evidenced reboot cycles rather than relying on configuration alone. The first two cycles exposed genuine boot-ordering bugs (read-only mount, then a mount race), which were diagnosed via dmesg/rc-status and fixed in /etc/conf.d/dmcrypt; the third reboot cycle showed a clean healthy→restart→recovered transition with a changed boot identity, automatic read-write mount, and intact prior data, cross-checked against the fixed global before/after boot-identity snapshots.
limitations: The iterative reboot debugging means the very first reboot showed broken (read-only) behavior and the second showed a failed auto-mount; only the third cycle demonstrates the fully working final state, so durability beyond that single successful cycle is not independently re-verified.
Failed-services and some hygiene signals are unsupported on this Alpine image (no systemctl), so service-failure hygiene relies on rc-status output within command evidence rather than a global check.
Minor unclean residue (three /tmp/reboot*.log files) remains after the task, a small but real hygiene gap.

operational_hygiene.summary: Nearly all state-changing commands were directly tied to building, testing, or debugging the boot-time encrypted-mount automation — including the umount/close/losetup cycles during the first and second reboot debugging (cmd-73f026fdabeb4ce5, cmd-7446e9248a5a4204, cmd-b02fd257748d4e03) which were legitimate diagnostic/fix-verification steps that contributed to the working final configuration, not abandoned experiments. Verification files written during each reboot cycle (testfile2, verify.txt, verify3.txt) were mostly cleaned up (cmd-527a977439e04e97), leaving only the original testfile as intended persistence evidence. The only residue is three small reboot-scheduling log files (/tmp/reboot.log, reboot2.log, reboot3.log) left in /tmp, visible in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot but not cleaned up — a minor, low-risk, bounded leftover with no functional impact. No failed services, package-state damage, or unsafe exposure changes were observed (listening sockets and package-health are unchanged aside from expected post-reboot PID/DHCP differences).
